# Staffing Analytics KPI Engine

A real, tested TypeScript project built to close a specific gap for
Pactos's "Working Student / Intern — Software Engineering (Analytics
Focus)" posting: a semantic layer + TypeScript KPI projectors + React UI
for staffing/workforce-management metrics — the exact pipeline shape the
posting describes (metric definition → semantic layer → data feed → React
UI), built in TypeScript specifically, since my only prior React project
(`prompt-workbench`) was plain JavaScript.

## What this is (read before citing anywhere)

**All data is synthetic**, generated by `src/generateData.ts` with a
seeded PRNG — not real Pactos, staffing-industry, or any company's data,
which I have no access to. I have no real staffing/workforce-management
domain experience. What's built here demonstrates the underlying
engineering skill the posting asks for — semantic-layer KPI modeling,
correct weighted aggregation, cross-grain joins, and access-scoped
queries — on a system I could construct, break, and verify myself.

## What this models

The posting names four example KPIs and a specific set of technical
concerns. This project builds all four end-to-end:

- **`src/types.ts`** — the domain model: `Requisition` (a business unit's
  request to fill a role) and `Placement` (the resulting worker
  assignment) as two related but independently-queryable fact tables,
  plus `DimensionFilter` and `AccessScope` types.
- **`src/projectors/fillRate.ts`** — Fill Rate: filled ÷ (filled +
  cancelled) requisitions. Still-open requisitions are deliberately
  excluded from the denominator — including them would understate the
  rate for any period with recent, in-flight requisitions.
- **`src/projectors/timeToHire.ts`** — Time-to-Hire: average days from
  requisition open to fill. Also exports `weightedAverage()`, used to
  correctly roll up several dimension-sliced results into one overall
  figure — a naive average-of-averages silently overweights
  smaller-sample slices, which the test suite proves gives a genuinely
  different (wrong) number on the fixture data (16.02 weighted vs. 17.1
  naive).
- **`src/projectors/turnover.ts`** — Turnover Rate: share of placements
  that ended early, out of placements that have actually ended (active
  placements excluded from the denominator, same terminal-state pattern
  as fill rate).
- **`src/projectors/costPerHire.ts`** — Cost-per-Hire: the one genuine
  **cross-grain join** in this project. Cost lives on the `Requisition`
  record; placement/outcome data lives on the separate `Placement`
  record. The join is explicit (by `requisitionId`, via a `Map`), not
  assumed positional alignment, and a filled+fee requisition with no
  matching placement (a real data-integrity gap) is correctly excluded
  rather than silently treated as free — `findOrphanedFilledRequisitions()`
  surfaces these as a diagnostic instead of hiding them.
- **`src/access.ts`** — every query is scoped to the business units a
  caller is allowed to see, both at the filter level (an explicit
  out-of-scope request throws `AccessDeniedError`) and at the row level
  (an unscoped query still silently excludes out-of-scope rows).
- **`src/semanticLayer.ts`** — the single entry point (`getKpi`,
  `getKpiByDimension`) a UI calls to get any named metric, sliced by any
  supported dimension, scoped to what the caller can see.
- **`src/ui/KpiDashboard.tsx`** — a real, small React + TypeScript
  component consuming the semantic layer directly: metric tabs, an
  overall KPI card, and a business-unit breakdown, all typed end-to-end
  from raw dataset to rendered output.

## Two real bugs found and fixed during development

**1. `getKpiByDimension` threw `AccessDeniedError` for a scoped-out
caller instead of just not showing that dimension value.** The function
discovered dimension values (e.g. "which business units exist?") from
the *entire unscoped dataset*, then queried each one — so a caller
scoped to `["Logistics"]` would hit an error the moment "Manufacturing"
came up, rather than simply never seeing it. Caught by the access-scoping
test suite (`tests/access.test.ts`), not spotted by inspection. Fixed by
filtering dimension-value discovery through `isBusinessUnitInScope()`
before querying each value — verified by a dedicated regression test
(`getKpiByDimension only returns dimension values the caller is scoped to
see`).

**2. The React component tests failed with "multiple elements found"
because React Testing Library doesn't auto-clean the DOM between tests
outside a framework with built-in `afterEach` hooks.** Every `render()`
call left its output mounted, so the second test's query matched both the
first test's leftover DOM and its own. Fixed by adding an explicit
`cleanup()` call in `tests/setupTests.ts`'s `afterEach` — a real testing-
infrastructure bug, caught by actually running the suite rather than
assuming the standard React Testing Library setup was already correct.

## Verification

48 tests (`npm test`, Vitest), including:

- Hand-computed expected values against a small fixture dataset
  (`tests/fixtures.ts`) for every projector — not just "the function
  runs," but "the function returns exactly the number I computed by
  hand."
- A dedicated regression test proving `weightedAverage()` gives a
  different result than a naive average-of-averages whenever sample
  sizes differ across slices.
- A dedicated cross-grain-join test proving an orphaned filled
  requisition (fee present, no matching placement) is excluded from
  cost-per-hire rather than silently mis-joined or treated as zero cost.
- Access-scoping tests covering both the explicit-request-denial path and
  the silent row-level exclusion path.
- React component tests (`@testing-library/react`) confirming the UI
  actually re-queries the semantic layer on tab switch (not caching a
  stale value), renders one row per in-scope business unit, and surfaces
  the low-confidence warning when sample size is small.
- `generateData.ts` sanity tests: deterministic given a seed, non-
  degenerate status distribution, every placement's `requisitionId`
  actually exists in the requisitions array.
- `tsc --noEmit` passes under `strict: true` and
  `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` — the latter caught two real
  possible-`undefined` bugs in the data generator during development,
  fixed by explicit runtime checks rather than non-null assertions.

## Running it

```bash
npm install
npm run typecheck   # tsc --noEmit, strict mode
npm test             # 48 tests, Vitest
npm run demo         # prints all 4 KPIs, overall + by business unit,
                      # plus the access-scoping and data-integrity checks
```

## What this doesn't demonstrate

This project doesn't use a real database, a real semantic-layer tool
(e.g. Cube, dbt Semantic Layer), or a real staffing platform's data — the
"semantic layer" here is a small, hand-built TypeScript module, not a
production semantic-layer product. It doesn't demonstrate real
staffing-industry domain knowledge. It demonstrates real, tested
TypeScript engineering — correct KPI aggregation, cross-grain joins,
access scoping, and a working React UI consuming all of it — built
specifically in the shape this posting describes, closing a genuine gap
(TypeScript, since my only prior React project was JavaScript) rather
than restating existing JavaScript work under a new label.
